text: The Sun is about 150 million km from Earth (1 astronomical unit)
as_written: A hundred and fifty million kilometres away
source: NASA Sun and Earth fact sheets; IAU 2012 definition of the astronomical unit (149,597,870,700 m)

text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth
as_written: eight minutes and twenty seconds
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Sun facts

text: Active regions on the Sun can be larger than Earth
as_written: bigger than the whole Earth
source: NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory sunspot and active region imagery

text: Near solar maximum flares occur several times a day, over an eleven-year cycle
as_written: there are several a day
source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, solar cycle and flare statistics

text: The solar cycle lasts about 11 years
as_written: eleven-year cycle
source: NASA/NOAA Solar Cycle Prediction Panel

text: Flares heat gas to tens of millions of degrees
as_written: tens of millions of degrees
source: NASA Goddard, solar flare explainer

text: Coronal mass ejections carry billions of tonnes of plasma
as_written: a mass of billions of tonnes
source: NASA Heliophysics, coronal mass ejection fact sheet

text: Flare classes A, B, C, M, X are each ten times stronger than the previous; X starts at 1e-4 W/m2 in GOES 1-8 angstrom X-rays
as_written: The X class begins at one ten-thousandth of a watt per square metre
source: NOAA SWPC, GOES X-ray flux flare classification

text: The November 2003 flare saturated GOES detectors and was estimated at about X28
as_written: about X28
source: NOAA SWPC; Thomson et al. 2004, Geophysical Research Letters

text: One analysis estimated the 1859 Carrington flare near X45
as_written: near X45
source: Cliver and Dietrich 2013, Journal of Space Weather and Space Climate

text: The largest flares release up to about 1e32 erg, roughly 1e25 joules
as_written: ten trillion trillion joules
source: NASA Goddard, solar flare facts (up to 10^32 erg)

text: Earth intercepts less than one billionth of the energy emitted by a flare, from cross-section over a sphere at 1 AU
as_written: less than one billionth of that energy
source: Geometric calculation using NASA Earth fact sheet radius and 1 AU; fraction is about 4.5e-10

text: The D region of the ionosphere lies roughly 60 to 90 km up
as_written: roughly sixty to ninety kilometres up
source: NOAA SWPC, D-region absorption and HF radio

text: HF radio spans 3 to 30 megahertz
as_written: between three and thirty megahertz
source: ITU Radio Regulations frequency band designations

text: NOAA R5 extreme radio blackout corresponds to X20 or above and means complete HF blackout across the sunlit side for hours
as_written: X20 or above
source: NOAA Space Weather Scales, Radio Blackouts R5

text: December 2006 flare of about X6 disrupted GPS receivers
as_written: a flare of about X6
source: Cerruti et al. 2008, Space Weather, Effect of intense December 2006 solar radio bursts on GPS receivers

text: The fastest solar protons arrive within tens of minutes
as_written: within tens of minutes
source: NOAA SWPC, Solar Radiation Storms

text: Standard atmosphere mass above one square metre is about 10 tonnes, equal to about 10 m of water
as_written: about ten tonnes of air
source: International Standard Atmosphere, 101,325 Pa sea-level pressure

text: Only a few dozen ground level enhancements have been recorded since the 1940s
as_written: only a few dozen have been recorded since the 1940s
source: University of Oulu GLE database (neutron monitor network)

text: The February 1956 ground level enhancement raised neutron counts by well over 1,000 percent at some stations
as_written: well over a thousand percent at some stations
source: University of Oulu GLE database; Usoskin et al. on GLE 5

text: A major solar particle event occurred in August 1972 between Apollo 16 and 17, with potentially dangerous doses for crew on the Moon
as_written: In August 1972, between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions
source: NASA Science, Apollo-era solar particle event analyses

text: Geostationary orbit is about 6.6 Earth radii out; magnetopause is normally about 10 Earth radii and can be compressed inside it in extreme storms
as_written: about six and a half Earth radii
source: NOAA SWPC magnetosphere description; standard geostationary orbit radius

text: Typical CME speeds are a few hundred to about a thousand km/s
as_written: between a few hundred and about a thousand kilometres per second
source: NASA Heliophysics, CME fact sheet; SOHO LASCO CME catalog

text: The July 2012 CME travelled at around 2,500 km/s
as_written: around two and a half thousand kilometres per second
source: Baker et al. 2013, Space Weather, A major solar eruptive event in July 2012

text: The Carrington CME took about 17 hours
as_written: just seventeen hours or so
source: Cliver and Svalgaard 2004, Solar Physics (17.6 hours)

text: Spacecraft at L1 are about 1.5 million km sunward and give 15 to 60 minutes warning
as_written: between fifteen and sixty minutes
source: NOAA SWPC, DSCOVR and ACE at L1

text: Distance to L1 about 1.5 million km
as_written: one and a half million kilometres
source: NASA, Lagrange Point 1 mission pages (SOHO, DSCOVR)

text: An earlier CME in July 2012 likely cleared the path for the second
as_written: the first cloud cleared the way
source: Liu et al. 2014, Nature Communications

text: The July 2012 eruption missed Earth by about a week
as_written: about a week earlier
source: NASA Science news, Near Miss: The Solar Superstorm of July 2012

text: Dst of the March 1989 storm reached about -589 nT
as_written: about minus five hundred and eighty-nine
source: WDC for Geomagnetism, Kyoto, Dst index

text: Carrington storm Dst estimated between about -850 and -1760 nT
as_written: between about minus eight hundred and fifty and minus seventeen hundred and sixty
source: Siscoe et al. 2006 (about -850 nT); Tsurutani et al. 2003 (about -1760 nT), Journal of Geophysical Research

text: During the 1859 storm operators on the Boston to Portland line worked about two hours without batteries
as_written: for about two hours
source: Loomis 1861, American Journal of Science; Boteler 2006, Advances in Space Research

text: Auroras in 1859 reached the Caribbean
as_written: as far south as the Caribbean
source: Green and Boardsen 2006, Advances in Space Research; Kimball 1960 aurora catalogue

text: Hydro-Quebec grid collapsed in about 90 seconds on 13 March 1989 at 2:44 am
as_written: In about ninety seconds
source: NERC, March 13 1989 Geomagnetic Disturbance report; Hydro-Quebec

text: Six million people lost power in the 1989 Quebec blackout
as_written: Six million people lost power
source: NASA Science, Quebec blackout; Hydro-Quebec

text: Restoration of most of the Quebec grid took about nine hours
as_written: about nine hours
source: NERC 1990 report on the March 1989 GMD

text: A transformer at the Salem nuclear plant in New Jersey was damaged in March 1989
as_written: a large transformer at a nuclear plant in New Jersey was damaged
source: NERC 1990 report on the March 1989 GMD

text: Malmo, Sweden lost power for under an hour affecting about 50,000 customers in October 2003
as_written: about fifty thousand customers for under an hour
source: Pulkkinen et al. 2005, Space Weather, Halloween storm impacts on power systems

text: Lloyd's 2013 estimated 20 to 40 million people at risk of outage lasting 16 days to 1 to 2 years, costing $0.6 to $2.6 trillion
as_written: between twenty and forty million people could lose power
source: Lloyd's and Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Solar Storm Risk to the North American Electric Grid, 2013

text: Lloyd's cost range of 0.6 to 2.6 trillion dollars
as_written: between six hundred billion and two point six trillion dollars
source: Lloyd's and AER 2013

text: Lloyd's outage duration range of 16 days to 1 to 2 years
as_written: from sixteen days to one or two years
source: Lloyd's and AER 2013

text: US National Research Council 2008 estimated $1 to 2 trillion in the first year and 4 to 10 years recovery
as_written: one to two trillion dollars in the first year, and a recovery of four to ten years
source: National Research Council 2008, Severe Space Weather Events: Understanding Societal and Economic Impacts

text: Large power transformers can take more than a year to deliver
as_written: can take more than a year to deliver
source: US Department of Energy, Large Power Transformer Resilience reports

text: SpaceX launched 49 Starlink satellites in February 2022 and 38 were lost
as_written: forty-nine Starlink satellites
source: SpaceX Starlink update, 8 February 2022

text: 38 of the satellites fell out of the sky
as_written: Thirty-eight of them fell out of the sky
source: SpaceX Starlink update, 8 February 2022

text: Parking orbit at about 210 km altitude
as_written: about two hundred and ten kilometres up
source: SpaceX Starlink update, 8 February 2022

text: Air density at that altitude up to 50 percent higher than earlier launches
as_written: up to fifty percent higher
source: SpaceX Starlink update, 8 February 2022

text: More than 10,000 working satellites are in orbit
as_written: more than ten thousand working satellites
source: Jonathan McDowell satellite catalog; Union of Concerned Scientists satellite database

text: May 2024 storm was the strongest in more than twenty years and disrupted precision farming GPS
as_written: the biggest in more than twenty years
source: NOAA SWPC, May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm assessment (G5, first since October 2003)

text: Ozone losses after the 1989 and 2003 solar particle events were measurable but modest
as_written: measurable but modest ozone losses
source: Jackman et al. 2005 and Seppala et al. 2006, solar proton event ozone studies

text: Riley estimated about a 12 percent chance per decade of a Carrington-class storm
as_written: about twelve percent per decade
source: Riley 2012, Space Weather, On the probability of occurrence of extreme space weather events

text: Miyake found a roughly 1.2 percent carbon-14 jump in 774 to 775 CE tree rings, about 20 times normal variation
as_written: a jump of about one point two percent
source: Miyake et al. 2012, Nature, A signature of cosmic-ray increase in AD 774-775 from tree rings in Japan

text: The jump was roughly twenty times larger than normal yearly change
as_written: roughly twenty times larger than the normal year-to-year change
source: Miyake et al. 2012, Nature

text: Beryllium-10 and chlorine-36 in polar ice cores corroborate the event
as_written: beryllium-10 and chlorine-36
source: Mekhaldi et al. 2015, Nature Communications

text: A short gamma-ray burst was proposed as an alternative cause
as_written: a short gamma-ray burst from far away
source: Hambaryan and Neuhauser 2013, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

text: Further spikes found in 993 CE, 660 BCE and about 5259 BCE
as_written: 993, in 660 before the common era, and around 5259 before the common era
source: Miyake et al. 2013 (993 CE); Park et al. 2017 (660 BCE); Miyake et al. 2017 (5259 BCE)

text: Roughly a dozen such events are known over the last twelve thousand years or so
as_written: Roughly a dozen are now known
source: Usoskin 2023, Living Reviews in Solar Physics, A history of solar activity over millennia

text: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 774 describes a red crucifix in the sky after sunset, possibly an aurora
as_written: a red crucifix in the sky after sunset
source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for 774; discussed in Usoskin et al. 2013, Astronomy and Astrophysics

text: Sun-like stars produce superflares about once per century on average
as_written: about once per century on average
source: Vasilyev et al. 2024, Science, Sun-like stars produce superflares roughly once per century
